title: System and method for determining relevancy of query responses in a distributed network search mechanism

report.headline: Dead patent with a future (66/100, high confidence): an expired federated-search ranking method in a field that is still very much alive, but crowded with later patents and modern ML ranking.
report.what_it_is: This patent describes a way to send one search query to many separate systems, collect their answers in a shared format, and merge them into a single list ranked by relevance. Think of one search box that asks many databases at once and sorts all their answers together.

why_it_died.text: It did not die early. It ran its full term and expired on 2022-10-14. The owner paid every maintenance fee, which suggests it was valued to the end rather than abandoned for lack of merit. That is why 'Died for money, not merit' scores only partially (7.5/15): it simply aged out.

case_for.point: The core problem is still a real product feature. Enterprise tools today sell 'one query across many systems, merged results.'
The patent was heavily relied on by others: cited by 227 later filings and used by examiners against 139 applications. That is why it scores full marks on examiner relevance.
Its claims were broad at grant. The first claim covers the general idea of merging ranked responses from many providers using a common protocol. This drives the high breadth score (13.9/15).
The owner kept paying fees until the end and filed in 3 jurisdictions, signals that the idea had commercial value.

case_against.point: Momentum has faded. Only 2 citing filings date from 2019 on, and none from unrelated owners after expiry. Recent momentum scores just 8.6/20.
The space is mature and contested. Other patents cover merging results from multiple engines and choosing which engines to query.
Newer work ranks federated results with machine learning, so the 2001 architecture alone may not be a differentiator.
Companies already ship this capability, so a founder would compete with established enterprise search vendors.

blockers.point: 40 later patents by other owners were cited against this one and may still be in force. They may cover parts of what you would build.
Software search is a dense patent field. Large incumbents file often. Related patents on multi-engine merging and federation exist.
If you search across customer data, privacy rules like GDPR, HIPAA or CCPA may apply.
The patent gives the idea, not a working system. Expect to build ranking, connectors and protocol details yourself.

assumption_to_test.assumption: Mid-size companies will pay a new vendor for federated search across their internal systems, even though enterprise platforms already offer it.
assumption_to_test.why_riskiest: The base architecture is old and already sold by vendors like Accuris, and recent work focuses on ML ranking. If buyers feel existing tools solve this, there is no business regardless of the patent.
assumption_to_test.how_to_test: In two weeks, run 10-15 interviews with IT or knowledge-management leads at 100-2,000 person companies. Ask how they search across systems today, what it costs, and what is broken. Pair this with a $200-300 landing page with a 'request pilot' button aimed at one niche (e.g. engineering docs). Success bar: at least 3 people describe a painful, unsolved gap and 2 ask for a pilot.

attorney_questions: Which of the 40 later patents cited against US6961723B2, and patents like US7984039 and US7930286, appear to still be in force and worth reviewing for our planned product?
Does the full expiry of US6961723B2 and its related family members in 3 jurisdictions affect what we should check before building in the US and abroad?
If we add machine-learning ranking on top of federated search, what recent filings (such as US11989192) should we review, and is our own approach worth considering for protection?
report.disclaimer: Research and triage only, not legal advice. This report is not a patentability, validity or freedom-to-operate opinion. Patent status shown here comes from public records that can lag or be wrong. An expired patent is not the same as free to use: follow-on patents, regulatory exclusivity, trade secrets and standards can still block a product. Confirm with a registered patent attorney before acting.

signals.signal: Historically strong technical influence: the patent was widely cited, including heavily by examiners, indicating it sat near the core of distributed/federated search prior art.
Recent citation momentum is weak: very few citing filings since 2019 and none from unrelated owners after expiry, suggesting the specific approach is now less of a reference point for new filings.
The underlying problem of federating queries across multiple sources and ranking merged results remains commercially and technically active, including ML-based ranking approaches.
The owner valued the patent through full term and it was filed in multiple jurisdictions, and the revival score rates the field as still alive.

read.who_is_active: Autobrains Technologies is the only company in the evidence filing on top of this patent since 2019, while Accuris markets federated search in its Goldfire enterprise platform.
read.market_read: Federated search with result merging and ranking is still a live product capability and research area, though recent work appears to have moved toward machine-learning ranking rather than building directly on this patent. A founder should treat this as a mature, contested space where differentiation will likely come from modern ranking and enterprise integration rather than the base architecture, and should confirm any plans with qualified counsel.

web.finding: Accuris describes a federated search capability in its Goldfire enterprise search platform that runs one query across multiple internal systems at once and aggregates the results.
USPTO patent US7984039 claims merging results from multiple search engines by ranking each engine's results with a per-query merit score.
USPTO patent US7930286 describes a federator that chooses which search engines to send a query to and gathers their ranked results.
USPTO patent US11989192, a recent federated search system, ranks matched groups from different data sources using machine learning models, a sign that work on this problem continues.
